introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0765 Pure Maths with Mechanics 1, June 2024, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL questions; each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D and only one answer must be marked (if more than one answer is marked the score for that question is zero). Formulae booklets and calculators are allowed. Section A: Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35); Section B: Mechanics (questions 36 to 50). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. The scan is complete: cover page and five pages of questions (pages 2 to 6), questions numbered 1 to 50.

Question convertie en ouverte ; la réponse visée par les correcteurs est probablement l'option C.

Question 47 : le signe entre 6t et (1/2)t^2 est dégradé sur le scan (point au lieu d'un trait) ; il est lu comme un moins, seule lecture compatible avec « decelerating to rest » (v = 6t - t^2/2 s'annule à t = 12). Deux instants donnent v = 10 (t = 2, accélération +4, et t = 10, accélération -4) ; « the deceleration » est lu comme la décélération en t = 10, soit 4 m/s2 (option A). L'option D (-4 m/s2) est l'accélération, pas la décélération : la clé A suppose que les correcteurs donnent la valeur positive.

Forces lues sur la figure : en B réaction normale 9 N (horizontale, loin du mur) et frottement 8 N vers le haut ; poids 40 N au milieu ; en A réaction 32 N vers le haut et frottement 9 N vers le mur. Les équilibres vertical (32 + 8 = 40) et horizontal (9 = 9) sont vérifiés, ce qui confirme la lecture ; l'équation des moments en A donne tan(theta) = 4/3 (option A).

Question 10 : l'exposant est lu comme r - 1 (somme de m/2^(r-1) pour r de 1 à l'infini), soit 2m = 10 et m = 5 (option B). Question 14 : y = 2/t (le t imprimé ressemble à un « ι »). Question 2 : la base du logarithme est x (log_x y = 2).

Question 31 : « the complete expansion is valid » est lu comme le domaine de validité usuel du développement binomial d'une puissance non entière, |x/3| < 1 soit -3 < x < 3 (option B ; les bornes sont exclues par convention).

Question 49 : g n'est pas donné dans l'énoncé ; la réponse n'en dépend pas (T = 14 a = 42 N, force sur la poulie 42 racine de 2 N), et elle est cohérente avec g = 10 m/s2 (6g - T = 6a). Question 45 : g = 10 m/s2 est imposé par l'énoncé ; la puissance 69 kW est lue 69 000 W.

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 17. Question 17 : l'ensemble exact des k est -1/2 <= k <= 2 (bornes incluses), absent des options (l'option C est l'intervalle ouvert).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

Given the functions $f, g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ where $f(x)=x^2-1$ and $g(x)=2x+1$, $(g\circ f)(2)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $(g\circ f)(2)=g(f(2))$: first $f(2)=2^2-1=3$, then $g(3)=2(3)+1=7$. The order matters: $(f\circ g)(2)=f(5)=24$ (option C) is the result of applying the functions in the wrong order. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\log_x y=2$ and $xy=125$, then the values of $x$ and $y$ are respectively
questions.corrige_markdown: $\log_x y=2$ means $y=x^2$ (with $x>0$, $x\neq1$). Substituting in $xy=125$ gives $x\cdot x^2=x^3=125$, so $x=5$ and $y=x^2=25$. Check: $\log_5 25=2$ and $5\times25=125$. Option D swaps the two values ($\log_{25}5=\tfrac12\neq2$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The vertical asymptotes of the curve $y=\dfrac{1}{(x-2)(x+3)}$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator vanishes and the numerator does not: $(x-2)(x+3)=0$ gives $x=2$ and $x=-3$ (the numerator is the constant $1$, never zero). Options A, C and D come from sign errors when reading the roots off the factors. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When the polynomial $p(x)=ax^3+5x^2+2x-8$ is divided by $(x-1)$, the remainder is $-3$. $a=$
questions.corrige_markdown: By the remainder theorem the remainder on division by $(x-1)$ is $p(1)$. So $p(1)=a+5+2-8=a-1=-3$, which gives $a=-2$. Option C ($a=2$) comes from a sign error. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The set of values of $x$ for which $\dfrac{(x+1)^2+3}{(x+3)(x-2)}<0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The numerator $(x+1)^2+3\ge3>0$ for every real $x$, so the sign of the fraction is the sign of the denominator. The fraction is negative exactly when $(x+3)(x-2)<0$, that is $-3<x<2$ (the quadratic $(x+3)(x-2)$ has a positive leading coefficient, so it is negative between its roots). The endpoints are excluded: at $x=2$ and $x=-3$ the fraction is undefined, so option C is wrong; options A and B describe where the fraction is positive. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is defined by

$$
f(x)=\begin{cases}4\beta+4x, & x<1\\ 4x-\beta^2-4, & x>1\end{cases}
$$

If $f(x)$ has a limit at $x=1$, the value of $\beta$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The limit exists when the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal. Left: $\lim_{x\to1^-}f(x)=4\beta+4$. Right: $\lim_{x\to1^+}f(x)=4-\beta^2-4=-\beta^2$. Setting them equal: $4\beta+4=-\beta^2$, i.e. $\beta^2+4\beta+4=0$, i.e. $(\beta+2)^2=0$, so $\beta=-2$ (a double root). Check: both one-sided limits equal $-4$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Let $p$ and $q$ be statements.

| $p$ | $q$ | $\oplus$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | T |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | F |

The compound statement $\oplus$ on the table could represent
questions.corrige_markdown: The column $\oplus$ is false only when both $p$ and $q$ are false, which is the truth table of the disjunction $p\lor q$ (true when at least one of them is true). $p\to q$ would be false on the row T, F; $p\leftrightarrow q$ would be false on rows T, F and F, T; $p\land q$ would be true only on the first row. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the lines

$L_1:\ \mathbf r=3\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+4\mathbf k+\lambda(4\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-3\mathbf k)$

$L_2:\ \mathbf r=\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+\mathbf k+\delta(8\mathbf i+4\mathbf j-6\mathbf k)$

$L_3:\ \mathbf r=2\mathbf i+6\mathbf j+2\mathbf k+\beta(\mathbf i-4\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)$

$L_4:\ \mathbf r=4\mathbf i+12\mathbf j+4\mathbf k-\mu(\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+\mathbf k)$.

Which pair of lines are parallel?
questions.corrige_markdown: Two lines are parallel when their direction vectors are scalar multiples of each other. Directions: $L_1:(4,2,-3)$; $L_2:(8,4,-6)=2(4,2,-3)$; $L_3:(1,-4,4)$; $L_4:(1,3,1)$ (the minus sign in front of $\mu$ only reverses it). Only $L_1$ and $L_2$ have proportional directions; $L_3$ and $L_4$ are proportional to none of the others (for example $(1,3,1)$ is not a multiple of $(4,2,-3)$). $L_1$ and $L_2$ are distinct parallel lines, since $(1,3,1)-(3,-2,4)=(-2,5,-3)$ is not a multiple of $(4,2,-3)$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A relation $R$ defined on a non-empty set $S$ is called a partial order if $R$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: By definition a partial order is a relation that is reflexive, anti-symmetric and transitive (for example $\le$ on $\mathbb R$, or $\subseteq$ on sets). Option C describes an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive). A relation that is both symmetric and anti-symmetric can only relate an element to itself, so options A and D do not define a partial order. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{m}{2^{r-1}}=10$, then $m=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Factor out the constant $m$: $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{m}{2^{r-1}}=m\left(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\cdots\right)$. The bracket is a geometric series with first term $1$ and common ratio $\tfrac12$ ($|r|<1$), whose sum to infinity is $\dfrac{1}{1-\frac12}=2$. So $2m=10$ and $m=5$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The first order differential equation obtained from the function $y=Ax+\ln x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Eliminate the arbitrary constant $A$. Differentiate: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=A+\dfrac1x$, so $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=Ax+1$. From the original function $Ax=y-\ln x$. Therefore $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y-\ln x+1$. Check with $y=Ax+\ln x$: $x(A+\tfrac1x)=Ax+1=y-\ln x+1$. Option A has the wrong sign of $\ln x$; option B omits the factor $x$ in front of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$; option C has $\ln(x+1)$ instead of $\ln x$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The shaded region represents

![fig-1](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: In the Venn diagram the shading lies inside the circle $B$ but outside the circle $A$ (the overlap of the two circles is left unshaded). The points that are in $B$ and not in $A$ form $A'\cap B$. $A\cap B$ would be the overlap itself, $A\cap B'$ the part of $A$ outside $B$, and $(A\cup B)'$ everything outside both sets. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is given by $f(x)=\dfrac{x+6}{x^2-2x-15}$. The domain of $f$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The function is defined for all real $x$ except where the denominator is zero. $x^2-2x-15=(x-5)(x+3)=0$ gives $x=5$ or $x=-3$. The numerator $x+6$ vanishes at $x=-6$, which is not a root of the denominator, so no factor cancels and both $-3$ and $5$ stay excluded. Domain: $\mathbb R-\{-3,5\}$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A curve is defined parametrically by $x=2t,\ y=\dfrac2t$. The Cartesian equation of the curve is
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply the two parametric equations: $xy=2t\cdot\dfrac2t=4$ (for $t\neq0$). The Cartesian equation is the rectangular hyperbola $xy=4$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\mathbf r=\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf s=-2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+\mathbf k$, then $\mathbf r\times\mathbf s$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\mathbf r\times\mathbf s=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&2&2\\-2&3&1\end{vmatrix}=\mathbf i(2\cdot1-2\cdot3)-\mathbf j(1\cdot1-2\cdot(-2))+\mathbf k(1\cdot3-2\cdot(-2))=-4\mathbf i-5\mathbf j+7\mathbf k$. The classic slip is forgetting the minus sign in front of the $\mathbf j$ component (options B and D). Check: the result is perpendicular to $\mathbf r$: $-4-10+14=0$, and to $\mathbf s$: $8-15+7=0$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $f(\theta)=\sin\theta-\sqrt3\cos\theta$. Expressing $f(\theta)$ in the form $R\sin(\theta-\alpha)$ where $R>0$ and $\alpha$ is an acute angle, we obtain $f(\theta)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand $R\sin(\theta-\alpha)=R\cos\alpha\sin\theta-R\sin\alpha\cos\theta$ and compare with $\sin\theta-\sqrt3\cos\theta$: $R\cos\alpha=1$ and $R\sin\alpha=\sqrt3$. Then $R=\sqrt{1^2+(\sqrt3)^2}=2$ and $\tan\alpha=\sqrt3$, so $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ (acute). Hence $f(\theta)=2\sin\left(\theta-\dfrac\pi3\right)$. Options B and D have $R=\sqrt{10}$, which would need $R^2=10$; option A has $\alpha=\pi/2$, which gives $2\sin(\theta-\pi/2)=-2\cos\theta$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If $f(x)=x^2+kx-3$ has a root in the interval $[1,2]$, then the range of $k$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $k<-\dfrac12$   B) $k>2$   C) $-\dfrac12<k<2$   D) $k<-\dfrac12$ or $k>2$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The product of the roots is $-3<0$, so the equation has exactly one positive root and one negative root; a root in $[1,2]$ must be the positive one. Since $f(0)=-3<0$ and $f(x)\to\infty$, $f$ is negative on $[0,r)$ and positive after the positive root $r$, so $r\in[1,2]$ exactly when $f(1)\le0\le f(2)$. Now $f(1)=k-2$ and $f(2)=2k+1$, so we need $k-2\le0$ and $2k+1\ge0$, which gives $-\tfrac12\le k\le2$. The endpoints are attained: $k=2$ gives the root $x=1$ and $k=-\tfrac12$ gives the root $x=2$. The examiners' intended answer is the open range of option C, but a root in the closed interval $[1,2]$ requires the closed range $-\tfrac12\le k\le2$, which is not among the options.

**Intended answer: C ($-\dfrac12<k<2$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that the sum and product of roots of the equation $2x^2-2x+q=0$ are equal, the value of $q$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For $ax^2+bx+c=0$ the sum of the roots is $-\dfrac ba$ and the product is $\dfrac ca$. Here the sum is $-\dfrac{-2}{2}=1$ and the product is $\dfrac q2$. Equal: $\dfrac q2=1$, so $q=2$. (The equation is then $x^2-x+1=0$ with complex roots $\dfrac{1\pm i\sqrt3}{2}$, but the sum and product relations still hold.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic progression is $n(2n+3)$. The $n^{\text{th}}$ term of the progression is
questions.corrige_markdown: $S_n=2n^2+3n$. For $n\ge2$, $u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=2n^2+3n-\left[2(n-1)^2+3(n-1)\right]=2n^2+3n-2n^2+4n-2-3n+3=4n+1$. For $n=1$: $u_1=S_1=5=4(1)+1$, so the formula holds for all $n\ge1$. Check: $u_1+u_2=5+9=14=S_2=2(7)$. The common difference is $4$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\left|\dfrac{-5+10i}{1+2i}\right|=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The modulus of a quotient is the quotient of the moduli: $|-5+10i|=\sqrt{25+100}=\sqrt{125}$ and $|1+2i|=\sqrt5$, so the value is $\sqrt{125}/\sqrt5=\sqrt{25}=5$. Check by division: $\dfrac{-5+10i}{1+2i}=\dfrac{(-5+10i)(1-2i)}{5}=\dfrac{15+20i}{5}=3+4i$, whose modulus is $5$. Option C is the modulus of the numerator only. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The line $L$ has equation $\mathbf r=5\mathbf i-8\mathbf j+\mathbf k+\lambda(\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$ and the plane $\pi$ has equation $2x+2y-z=5$. The sine of the acute angle between the line and the plane is
questions.corrige_markdown: Direction of the line $\mathbf d=(1,3,2)$, $|\mathbf d|=\sqrt{14}$. Normal to the plane $\mathbf n=(2,2,-1)$, $|\mathbf n|=3$. The angle $\varphi$ between a line and a plane satisfies $\sin\varphi=\dfrac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$ (it is the complement of the angle between $\mathbf d$ and $\mathbf n$). $\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=2+6-2=6$, so $\sin\varphi=\dfrac{6}{3\sqrt{14}}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{14}}=\dfrac{2\sqrt{14}}{14}=\dfrac{\sqrt{14}}{7}$. The other options are impossible for a sine: $\dfrac{3\sqrt{14}}{7}\approx1.60$, $\dfrac{2\sqrt{14}}{7}\approx1.07$ and $\dfrac{4\sqrt{14}}{7}\approx2.14$ all exceed $1$, while $\dfrac{\sqrt{14}}{7}\approx0.53$. **Answer: B.**

By the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(3x+2)^4=4(3x+2)^3\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}(3x+2)=4(3x+2)^3\cdot3=12(3x+2)^3$. Option A multiplies by an extra $x$, option B keeps the power $4$ and option D divides by $3$ instead of multiplying. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equation of the circle which passes through the origin and the points $(2,0)$ and $(0,-4)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: A circle through the origin has the form $x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey=0$. At $(2,0)$: $4+2D=0$, so $D=-2$. At $(0,-4)$: $16-4E=0$, so $E=4$. The circle is $x^2+y^2-2x+4y=0$, i.e. $(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=5$ with centre $(1,-2)$ and radius $\sqrt5$. Check: the angle at the origin is a right angle, so the segment from $(2,0)$ to $(0,-4)$ is a diameter with midpoint $(1,-2)$. Options B, C and D have wrong signs and fail one of the point tests. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The area of the finite region bounded by the curve $y=2x-\dfrac1x$ and the lines $x=1$ and $x=3$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: On $[1,3]$ the curve is above the $x$-axis: $2x-\tfrac1x\ge 1>0$ at $x=1$ and it is increasing. Area $=\displaystyle\int_1^3\left(2x-\frac1x\right)dx=\left[x^2-\ln x\right]_1^3=(9-\ln3)-(1-\ln1)=8-\ln3$. The sign of the logarithm term is negative because the curve is $2x$ minus $\dfrac1x$ (option B adds it). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If a root of the equation $x^2+2x+1=0$ is also a root of the equation $x^3-2x^2+6x+k=0$, the value of the constant $k$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $x^2+2x+1=(x+1)^2=0$ has the double root $x=-1$. Substitute $x=-1$ in the cubic: $(-1)^3-2(-1)^2+6(-1)+k=-1-2-6+k=0$, so $k=9$. Option B is the value of $-1-2-6$ without moving it to the other side. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A periodic function $f$ of period $4$ is defined by

$$
f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2, & 0\le x<2\\ x+2, & 2\le x<4\end{cases}
$$

$f(9)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Period $4$ means $f(x+4)=f(x)$, so $f(9)=f(9-8)=f(1)$. Since $0\le1<2$, $f(1)=1^2=1$. Option C is the value $9+2$ obtained by ignoring the periodicity and using the second rule, and option D is $9^2$ using the first rule. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two functions $f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ are such that $f(x)=2x-1$ and $(f\circ g)(x)=x-2$. Then $g(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $(f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))=2g(x)-1=x-2$. So $2g(x)=x-1$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{2}$. Check: $f\left(\dfrac{x-1}{2}\right)=(x-1)-1=x-2$. Option D is $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{2}$, which would give $(f\circ f^{-1})(x)=x$, not $x-2$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equation of the tangent to the curve $y=3x(2-x^2)$ at the point $(1,3)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $y=6x-3x^3$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=6-9x^2$, which equals $-3$ at $x=1$. The point $(1,3)$ is on the curve: $3(1)(2-1)=3$. Tangent: $y-3=-3(x-1)$, i.e. $y=-3x+6$, i.e. $3x+y-6=0$. Options A, C and D correspond to the slope $+3$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Simplifying $\dfrac{\sin5x-\sin x}{\sin4x-\sin2x}$ gives
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $\sin P-\sin Q=2\cos\dfrac{P+Q}{2}\sin\dfrac{P-Q}{2}$. Numerator: $\sin5x-\sin x=2\cos3x\sin2x$. Denominator: $\sin4x-\sin2x=2\cos3x\sin x$. The factor $2\cos3x$ cancels, leaving $\dfrac{\sin2x}{\sin x}=\dfrac{2\sin x\cos x}{\sin x}=2\cos x$. Numerical check at $x=\tfrac\pi4$: the quotient is $\dfrac{-\sqrt2}{-1}=\sqrt2=2\cos\dfrac\pi4$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word $ARREARS$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: ARREARS has $7$ letters: $A$ twice, $R$ three times, $E$ once and $S$ once. The number of distinct arrangements is $\dfrac{7!}{2!\,3!}=\dfrac{5040}{12}=420$. Option D ($840=7!/3!$) forgets to divide by $2!$ for the repeated $A$, and option A ($210$) divides by one factor too many ($7!/4!$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In the expansion of $\sqrt{3+x}$, the range of values of $x$ for which the complete expansion is valid is
questions.corrige_markdown: Write $\sqrt{3+x}=\sqrt3\left(1+\dfrac x3\right)^{1/2}$. The binomial series of $(1+u)^{n}$ for a non-integer $n$ is valid for $|u|<1$. With $u=\dfrac x3$ this gives $\left|\dfrac x3\right|<1$, so $-3<x<3$. Option C comes from forgetting to factor out $3$ (it would be the range for $(1+x)^{1/2}$) and option D from inverting $\dfrac x3$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Evaluating $1+\dfrac13+\dfrac19+\dfrac1{27}+\cdots$ gives
questions.corrige_markdown: This is a geometric series with first term $a=1$ and common ratio $r=\dfrac13$, $|r|<1$, so the sum to infinity is $\dfrac{a}{1-r}=\dfrac{1}{1-\frac13}=\dfrac32$. Option C, $\dfrac{40}{27}$, is only the sum of the first four terms; option D is $\dfrac1{1-\frac23}$ with the wrong ratio. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(\dfrac{4x^2-1}{2x^2+1}\right)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Divide numerator and denominator by $x^2$: $\dfrac{4-\frac1{x^2}}{2+\frac1{x^2}}\to\dfrac42=2$ as $x\to\infty$. The limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients because the degrees are equal. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_1^4\left(\dfrac{x+3}{x}\right)dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Split the integrand: $\dfrac{x+3}{x}=1+\dfrac3x$. Then $\displaystyle\int_1^4\left(1+\frac3x\right)dx=\left[x+3\ln x\right]_1^4=(4+3\ln4)-(1+0)=3+3\ln4$. Option D forgets to subtract the lower limit value $1$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the matrix $\mathbf M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\-1&-1&2\\-1&3&4\end{pmatrix}$, then the determinant of $\mathbf M$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand along the first row: $\det\mathbf M=1\begin{vmatrix}-1&2\\3&4\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}-1&2\\-1&4\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}-1&-1\\-1&3\end{vmatrix}=1(-4-6)-2(-4+2)+3(-3-1)=-10+4-12=-18$. Option D is the same number with the wrong sign, a typical slip in the alternating signs of the cofactors. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: MECHANICS**

The position vector of a particle at time $t$ seconds is $\mathbf r$, where $\mathbf r=\left[(t^2+1)\mathbf i+t^3\mathbf j\right]\ \mathrm m$. The velocity of the particle when $t=2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The velocity is the derivative of the position vector: $\mathbf v=\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=2t\,\mathbf i+3t^2\mathbf j$. At $t=2$: $\mathbf v=4\mathbf i+12\mathbf j\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Option A uses $3t$ instead of $3t^2$ for the $\mathbf j$ component, and option C uses $t$ instead of $2t$ for the $\mathbf i$ component. **Answer: D.**

themes: elastic strings and potential energy mechanics
questions.enonce_markdown: The extension a force of $20\ \mathrm N$ produces in a spring of natural length $5\ \mathrm m$ whose modulus of elasticity is $150\ \mathrm N$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Hooke's law: tension $T=\dfrac{\lambda x}{l}$ with $\lambda=150\ \mathrm N$, $l=5\ \mathrm m$ and $T=20\ \mathrm N$. So $x=\dfrac{Tl}{\lambda}=\dfrac{20\times5}{150}=\dfrac{100}{150}=\dfrac23\ \mathrm m$. Option A ($\tfrac32$) is the reciprocal of the correct value, obtained by inverting the ratio. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The velocity of a particle $A$ relative to another $B$ is $(7\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Given that the velocity of $A$ is $(8\mathbf i+6\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The velocity of $B$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The velocity of $A$ relative to $B$ is ${}_A\mathbf v_B=\mathbf v_A-\mathbf v_B$. So $\mathbf v_B=\mathbf v_A-{}_A\mathbf v_B=(8\mathbf i+6\mathbf j)-(7\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)=\mathbf i+\mathbf j\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Option B is $-\mathbf v_B$, obtained by subtracting in the wrong order, and option A adds the two vectors. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $A$ and $B$ are events with $P(A)=\dfrac14$, $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac13$ and $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac1{12}$. $P(A\mid B)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: From $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$: $P(B)=\dfrac13-\dfrac14+\dfrac1{12}=\dfrac{4-3+1}{12}=\dfrac16$. Then $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\dfrac{1/12}{1/6}=\dfrac12$. Option C is $P(B)$ itself, and $P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{1/12}{1/4}=\dfrac13$ (option B) is the conditional probability in the wrong direction. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A small sphere of mass $0.6\ \mathrm{kg}$ is moving on a horizontal table with a speed of $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ when it collides with a fixed smooth wall perpendicular to the table surface. It rebounds with a speed of $\dfrac{15}{2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The coefficient of restitution between the sphere and the wall is
questions.corrige_markdown: The sphere hits the wall perpendicularly (a direct impact). For a fixed wall Newton's law of restitution gives $e=\dfrac{\text{speed of rebound}}{\text{speed of approach}}=\dfrac{15/2}{10}=\dfrac34$. The mass $0.6\ \mathrm{kg}$ is not needed. Options A and B are greater than $1$ (impossible, since $0\le e\le1$) and come from inverting the ratio. **Answer: D.**

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown: Three particles of masses $5\ \mathrm{kg}$, $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $m\ \mathrm{kg}$ lie on the $y$-axis at the points $(0,4)$, $(0,2)$ and $(0,5)$ respectively. The center of mass of the system is at the point $(0,4)$. The value of $m$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: All the particles are on the $y$-axis, so only the $y$-coordinate of the centre of mass matters: $\bar y=\dfrac{5(4)+3(2)+m(5)}{5+3+m}=4$. So $26+5m=4(8+m)=32+4m$, giving $m=6$. Check: $\dfrac{20+6+30}{14}=\dfrac{56}{14}=4$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A car wheel of radius $\dfrac12\ \mathrm m$ is moving at a speed of $\dfrac{10}{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Its angular speed in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Linear and angular speeds are related by $v=r\omega$, so $\omega=\dfrac vr=\dfrac{10/3}{1/2}=\dfrac{20}{3}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. Option B ($\tfrac53$) is $v\times r$ instead of $v/r$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A car accelerates uniformly from a velocity of $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in $6$ seconds on a straight road. The distance it covered is
questions.corrige_markdown: For uniform acceleration $s=\dfrac{u+v}{2}\,t=\dfrac{10+60}{2}\times6=35\times6=210\ \mathrm m$. Check with $a=\dfrac{60-10}{6}=\dfrac{25}{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$: $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2=60+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{25}{3}\cdot36=60+150=210\ \mathrm m$. Option A ($150$) is only the $\tfrac12at^2$ term. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A box contains ten green and six white marbles. A marble is chosen at random, its colour noted and it is not replaced. This process is repeated once. The probability that the marbles chosen are of the same colour is
questions.corrige_markdown: There are $16$ marbles. Two green: $\dfrac{10}{16}\times\dfrac{9}{15}=\dfrac{90}{240}$. Two white: $\dfrac6{16}\times\dfrac5{15}=\dfrac{30}{240}$. These cases are mutually exclusive, so $P(\text{same colour})=\dfrac{90+30}{240}=\dfrac{120}{240}=\dfrac12$. Option A ($\tfrac{17}{32}$) is what one gets when the marble is replaced: $\left(\tfrac58\right)^2+\left(\tfrac38\right)^2=\dfrac{34}{64}=\dfrac{17}{32}$. **Answer: C.**

themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance
questions.enonce_markdown: The engine of a car of mass $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ works at a constant rate of $69\ \mathrm{kW}$ up a road inclined at an angle $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac16\right)$ to the horizontal. Given that the non-gravitational resistance to the motion of the car is $300\ \mathrm N$ and taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the maximum speed of the car is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take the direction up the slope as positive. The maximum speed is reached when the acceleration is zero, so the driving force $F$ balances the resistance and the component of the weight down the slope: $F=mg\sin\alpha+R=1200\times10\times\dfrac16+300=2000+300=2300\ \mathrm N$. The power is $P=Fv$, so $v=\dfrac{P}{F}=\dfrac{69\,000}{2300}=30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (with $P=69\ \mathrm{kW}=69\,000\ \mathrm W$). If the resistance were forgotten one would obtain $69000/2000=34.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is not an option; the check $2300\times30=69\,000\ \mathrm W$ confirms the answer. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The work done by a force $\mathbf F=(\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-4\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ which moves its point of application from a point $A$ with position vector $\mathbf r_A=(3\mathbf i-4\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$ to another point $B$ with position vector $\mathbf r_B=(-\mathbf i-6\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The work done by a constant force is $W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d$ where $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A=(-1-3)\mathbf i+(0+4)\mathbf j+(-6-0)\mathbf k=-4\mathbf i+4\mathbf j-6\mathbf k$. So $W=(1)(-4)+(-2)(4)+(-4)(-6)=-4-8+24=12\ \mathrm J$. Using a position vector instead of the displacement gives a wrong value ($\mathbf r_B\cdot\mathbf F=23\ \mathrm J$, $\mathbf r_A\cdot\mathbf F=11\ \mathrm J$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle decelerating to rest has its speed $v\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at time $t$ seconds given by $v=6t-\dfrac12t^2$. The deceleration of the particle when $v=10$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Set $v=10$: $6t-\tfrac12t^2=10\iff t^2-12t+20=0\iff(t-2)(t-10)=0$, so $t=2$ or $t=10$. The acceleration is $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=6-t$. At $t=2$ the acceleration is $+4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$: the particle is speeding up, not decelerating. At $t=10$ the acceleration is $-4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$: the particle is slowing down (it comes to rest at $t=12$, where $v=0$). The deceleration is the magnitude of the retardation, $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The value $-4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ in option D is the acceleration, not the deceleration. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A uniform ladder $AB$, of length $2a$, rests in limiting equilibrium with its top end against a rough vertical wall and its lower end on a rough horizontal floor. The forces acting on the ladder are as shown in Fig. 1.

![fig-2](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

The angle $\theta$ which $AB$ makes with the floor is given by
questions.corrige_markdown: Forces read on the figure: at $B$ (top, on the wall) a normal reaction $9\ \mathrm N$ horizontal, away from the wall, and a friction $8\ \mathrm N$ upwards; at the midpoint the weight $40\ \mathrm N$ downwards; at $A$ (on the floor) a normal reaction $32\ \mathrm N$ upwards and a friction $9\ \mathrm N$ horizontal towards the wall. The figure is consistent: vertically $32+8=40$, horizontally $9=9$. Take moments about $A$. The ladder has length $2a$, so $B$ is $2a\cos\theta$ horizontally and $2a\sin\theta$ vertically from $A$, and the weight acts at horizontal distance $a\cos\theta$. The weight turns the ladder one way: $40\times a\cos\theta$. The $8\ \mathrm N$ friction at $B$ gives $8\times2a\cos\theta$ and the $9\ \mathrm N$ reaction at $B$ gives $9\times2a\sin\theta$, both in the opposite sense. Equilibrium: $40a\cos\theta=16a\cos\theta+18a\sin\theta$, so $24\cos\theta=18\sin\theta$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{24}{18}=\dfrac43$. Option C is impossible (a sine cannot exceed $1$), $\tan\theta=\tfrac34$ is the reciprocal slope, and $\sin\theta=\tfrac34$ would give $\tan\theta=\tfrac{3}{\sqrt7}\neq\tfrac43$. Check: $\theta=\arctan\tfrac43\approx53.1^\circ$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $14\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests on a smooth horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table to a particle of mass $6\ \mathrm{kg}$ which hangs freely. Given that the acceleration of the system is $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ when it is released from rest, the force exerted by the string on the pulley is
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $T$ be the tension. The string is light and passes over a smooth pulley, so the tension is the same on both sides. For the $14\ \mathrm{kg}$ particle (horizontal motion, smooth table): $T=14a=14\times3=42\ \mathrm N$. (Check with the hanging particle and $g=10$: $6g-T=6a$ gives $60-42=18=6\times3$.) The string leaves the pulley along a horizontal part and a vertical part, so the two pulls on the pulley are $42\ \mathrm N$ horizontal (towards the table) and $42\ \mathrm N$ vertical (downwards), at right angles. Their resultant has magnitude $\sqrt{42^2+42^2}=42\sqrt2\ \mathrm N$, directed at $45^\circ$ below the horizontal towards the table. Option C is the tension itself, not the force on the pulley. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A smooth sphere $A$ of mass $6\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ collides directly with a smooth sphere $B$ of mass $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the opposite direction. Given that the speed of $B$ after impact is $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the kinetic energy of $A$ after impact is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take the initial direction of motion of $A$ as positive, so the initial velocities are $+4$ for $A$ and $-2$ for $B$. After impact $B$ has speed $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. If its velocity were still $-2$ it would not have been affected by the collision, which is impossible (the spheres were approaching), so $B$ moves off in the direction of $A$: $v_B=+2$. Conservation of momentum: $6(4)+3(-2)=6v_A+3(2)$, so $18=6v_A+6$ and $v_A=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (Newton's law gives $e=\dfrac{v_B-v_A}{4-(-2)}=0$: the spheres move together after impact, which is allowed since $0\le e\le1$.) Kinetic energy of $A$: $\tfrac12\times6\times2^2=12\ \mathrm J$. Option A ($6\ \mathrm J$) is the kinetic energy of $B$ after impact ($\tfrac12\times3\times2^2$), i.e. the energy of the wrong sphere. **Answer: B.**
